samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the fixes the same sensible way: first stop wiping the form after a decline, then the silent grey Pay button, then the errors that appear on the first keystroke. B covers what A misses: it notes that the fields have no persistent labels, and it gives concrete replacement error wording for a field. A never mentions labels and only calls 'Invalid input' vague without offering better wording, so B covers more of the rubric. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers rank the fixes the same way: the decline wipe first, then the silent disabled button, then error timing. Neither adds visual restyling. A also points out the missing persistent labels and gives concrete replacement error wording ("Enter the 3 or 4 digits on the back of your card"). B never mentions labels and only asks for "plain messages" without example wording. Neither answer says the actual decline reason should be shown, only a generic declined message.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the fixes well, starting with the decline wipe and then the silent disabled button. Answer A never mentions that the fields have only placeholders for labels. Answer B covers that and also handles error timing more fully: it waits until Pay is pressed, then re-checks as the person edits, and it gives concrete replacement wording for 'Invalid input'. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers rank the fixes well: the decline wipe first, then the silent disabled button, then the first-keystroke error. Both also keep entered values and avoid visual restyling. Answer A wins because it catches the placeholder-only labels problem and recommends persistent labels, which Answer B misses entirely. A also gives a better replacement for 'Invalid input' ('Enter the 16 digits from the front of your card'). B's analytics guidance is somewhat richer, but that doesn't make up for the missing labels point.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers put the fixes in a similar order: the decline wipe first, then the disabled Pay button, then the early error, with labels, keyboard, autofill and the country list as smaller items. Neither pads with visual restyling. B criticises the vague 'Invalid input' text more directly, gives more concrete replacement messages, explains more clearly why placeholder-only labels hurt, and is more careful that its diagnosis needs analytics to confirm. A is stronger on showing the real decline reason, with example wording, but B is slightly better overall. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the fixes the same way, starting with the decline wipe, and both cover all six rubric items well. B edges ahead because it gives real decline-reason wording, adds an error summary, keeps the button disabled only while payment is processing, and offers a sensible plan for the engineering ticket. A's decline fix says to show a message but gives no example of the reason to show, and its labels point is a bit weaker than its other points.

A is better at marking prefilled values as suggestions and at not overriding manual edits, but it adds pay and overtime fields the context doesn't mention, plus a broad 'smart behaviors' section. B is tighter, hedges on data the tool may not have (breaks), and explicitly blocks or warns on past dates, though it never shows where a suggestion came from.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers prefill location, date, times, role and break from the given context, leave the employee blank for a good reason, and say prefilled values must stay editable without overwriting manual edits. B gives sharper reasons, such as a blank employee meaning an open shift and old notes being stale. However, its date fallback ('the day after their most recently created shift') could land in the past, and it brings in pay overrides the context doesn't support. A stays safer on dates, though it assumes availability data and adds a bit of general advice about button labels. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers prefill a solid set of fields from the given context, leave the employee blank for well-argued reasons, and require prefilled values to stay visible, editable and safe from overwriting manual edits. Answer A's date fallback, 'the day after their most recently created shift', could land in the past, which the rubric rules out; B uses the source view's day or today. B has its own flaws: it says it left thresholds out right after suggesting about 60%, it assumes availability data the context doesn't provide, and it drifts slightly into button labels.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers prefill location, date, times and role from the given context, and both leave the employee blank for good reasons. A is tighter and stays on this screen, though its table and its notes guidance contradict each other slightly. B is more thorough, with a fallback for thin data and pay-rate handling, but it adds generic metrics advice with arbitrary thresholds and assumes availability data the tool doesn't have; neither shows where a suggestion came from. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers prefill location, date, times and role from the given context, leave the employee blank because a wrong guess is costly, and say defaults should look like real, editable values. B explicitly keeps the date from being in the past and adds the useful 'Add another' flow. A goes a bit beyond the context by suggesting availability-based staff suggestions, and spends more on extras like metrics. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject the either/or framing and give concrete per-field behavior. Both also clear errors live once they appear, debounce the username check and use a hint for the password rule. A recommends validating on blur, so errors don't appear mid-typing and problems don't pile up at submit. B argues against blur and checks email only on submit, which misses the rubric's central recommendation, even though B adds useful extra details on accessibility and autofill. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B recommends checking each field when the person leaves it, then re-checking live once an error shows. That is the balanced approach the rubric asks for. A rejects checking on leaving the field, defaults email to submit-only and leans toward the designer, so it misses item 2. Both handle the username debounce and password hint well and give concrete behavior for each field.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B explains why both extremes fail: keystroke checks flag half-typed input, and submit-only checks leave errors such as a taken username until the end. It then recommends checking on blur, with errors shown only after a field has been touched and cleared live once fixed. A advises against checking on blur and gives a weak account of why submit-only fails, though its handling of each field (debounced username check, password checklist, errors that clear live) is strong. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A meets every rubric item. It explains why both extremes fail, recommends checking a field when the person leaves it, and says not to show errors on fields they haven't touched. Once an error shows, it re-checks as they type, and it gives specific handling for each of the three fields. Answer B has strong field-specific detail and accessibility advice, but it argues against checking on leaving a field and keeps submit as the main trigger, which goes against item 2. It also never names the main weakness of submit-only checking, which is a pile of errors at the end.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer A recommends checking a field once the person leaves it, then re-checking it live after an error appears, and it gives each field a concrete behavior, which covers the rubric well. Answer B has strong extras (accessibility, autocomplete, keeping the submit button active) and handles the username and password well. However, it explicitly rejects checking on leaving the field and leaves email to be checked only on submit. That goes against rubric item 2 and partly recreates the pile of errors at the end. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B explains both failure modes: false errors while someone is still typing, and a pile of problems discovered at submit. It recommends checking on blur, re-checking live once an error shows, a debounced username check that cancels stale requests, and showing the password rule up front. A does well on live re-checking and the per-field exceptions, but it explicitly rejects checking when someone leaves a field. It also leans on submit-only checking and barely mentions the problem of finding everything wrong at the end.
